name: Osteomyology

lead: Osteomyology is a form of manual therapy found almost only in the United Kingdom. It borrows from osteopathy and chiropractic and puts emphasis on relaxing muscles around the joints rather than working on bone alone. For appearance, the connection is posture: clients seek it to ease stiff backs, necks and shoulders so they can hold themselves more upright.

The term was coined in 1992 by osteopath Alan Clemens. No published research has examined osteomyology as a distinct practice; the manual techniques it draws on have been studied separately, with mixed results.

paras: Sessions are hands-on: practitioners use soft-tissue work and joint techniques similar to those of osteopaths and chiropractors, usually over a short course of visits. Practitioners describe the style as gentler and more participatory than classic manipulation.

Spinal manipulation commonly causes mild, short-lived soreness, and rarely serious harm, according to the general literature on the technique. Osteomyologists are not registered with the General Osteopathic Council or General Chiropractic Council; they self-regulate through their own association, and UK advertising regulators have acted on unsubstantiated claims by some practitioners.

angle.text: Clients seek osteomyology for stiffness in the back, neck and shoulders. Practitioners say loosening tight muscles helps people carry themselves more comfortably upright.

lead: Osteomyology is a hybrid manual-therapy practice, found almost exclusively in the United Kingdom, that combines elements of osteopathy and chiropractic with an emphasis on relaxing muscle [1]. People use bodywork of this kind to relieve tension in the back, neck and shoulders, which supports a more upright, relaxed posture and easier movement.

The name was coined in 1992 by English-born osteopath Alan Clemens, from Greek roots for bone and muscle, and grew out of an informal group of osteopaths and students seeking continuing training [1]. After UK laws in 1993 and 1994 protected the titles osteopath and chiropractor, practitioners who did not register with the statutory bodies increasingly adopted the label osteomyologist [1].

Practitioners say they focus on muscle relaxation and gentle technique. No reliable studies exist on osteomyology as a distinct practice, though research on its component manual therapies is mixed [1].
infobox: Self-regulated; not under GOsC or GCC

paras: Osteomyology draws loosely on chiropractic and osteopathy, and its practitioners are typically trained in one of those fields [1]. Proponents describe it as centred on relaxing muscles rather than manipulating bone, which they say is gentler and encourages patients to take part in their own recovery [1]. Critics note that the distinction from osteopathy is somewhat arbitrary [1].

The term was introduced in 1992 by Alan Clemens [1]. The UK's 1993 and 1994 acts protecting the titles osteopath and chiropractor led many unregistered practitioners to use osteomyologist instead [1]. Members of the Association of Osteomyologists use the designation MAO and the association sets its own membership rules [1].

No studies found on osteomyology as a distinct practice. Evidence for its component manual therapies is mixed, with some support for short-term relief of back pain and little for other conditions [1].

Spinal manipulation commonly produces mild, temporary side effects and, rarely, serious harm; the true rate is unknown [1]. Because osteomyologists are outside statutory regulation, clients have less formal protection [1]. The UK Advertising Standards Authority and the Committee of Advertising Practice have taken action over unsubstantiated claims, and some practitioners have been investigated for presenting themselves as osteopaths or chiropractors [1].
